body_markdown:
The wait is almost over. After teasing us with *[Neue Klasse](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/the-neue-klasse-concept-instills-hope-for-bmw-design/)* design studies and cars wrapped in camouflage, BMW has finally unwrapped the eighth-generation 3 Series.


Available in the U.S. beginning in early 2027, the new 3 will arrive as both a pure EV, known as the i3, and a gas mild-hybrid, with four- and six-cylinder power.


There’s no distinction from a design perspective between the electric and combustion-powered models, with both sharing BMW’s new design language that debuted on the[iX3](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bmw-ix3-to-start-at-61500-and-stop-at-434-miles/) e-SUV. The 3 Series sticks to its guns as a sports sedan, featuring a long wheelbase, short overhangs, and what BMW calls a 2.5-box design. The car’s stance and proportions lean towards the aggressive, but while there’s some subtle surfacing to the Neue Klasse method, it’s nothing like the Bangle days. The kidney grille is wider and thinner than ever before, effectively merging with the headlamps for a bold full-frontal look.


The 3 Series has grown in stature, being both longer and wider than its predecessor. There are very slight differences between the EV and ICE cars thanks to their architecture, but you’d have to look really close to spot them.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


In fact, it’d probably be easier to just listen for the difference. The near-silent running i3 50 XDrive features a 463-hp dual-motor, all-wheel drive powertrain and a 112.2 kWh battery pack that forms part of the vehicle structure. BMW claims a range of up to 468 miles and that, thanks to its 400-kW DC fast charging, you can add 208 miles in just ten minutes. Zero to 60 takes 4.5 seconds, while top speed is 124 mph.


BMW


To go faster, you’ll need the M350 xDrive with its three-liter turbocharged six, which doles out 437 hp at 5600-6500 rpm. Although that’s less than the i3, it’s also almost 800 pounds lighter, so it can hit 60 mph from a standstill in 3.9 seconds and max out at 155 mph. For something more sedate, and a little more frugal, there’s the two-liter, four-cylinder 330 with 255 hp at 4700-6500 rpm. It’ll still do the sprint to 60 in 5.9 seconds and reach the same 155 mph limited top speed. For extra traction, it too can be had with xDrive all-wheel drive. All ICE versions get an eight-speed Steptronic auto transmission and a 48-volt mild hybrid system.


Suspension is by a double-joint spring-strut front axle and a five-link rear axle, while an adaptive M Suspension system can be optioned. Also on M Performance cars are variable sport steering, M Sport differential, and M Sport brakes. A Drift Moment feature can be activated to send all the power to the rear wheels for sideways shenanigans.


BMW

BMW


Common to every 3 Series is a radical new cockpit, featuring BMW Panoramic Vision. This full-width digital display sits at the base of the windscreen and displays key information for the driver and passengers. A head-up driver display is optional, while the main touch-screen center display controls pretty much everything in the car, though there are physical buttons for the window switches, drive selector, parking brake, and HVAC, along with those on the steering wheel. It all looks very clean, but you’d better hope the voice activation understands your accent, or it could get a bit frustrating. In-car entertainment comes from a standard seven-speaker system, but if you opt for an M Performance model, you’ll get a Harmon Kardon hi-fi with Dolby Atmos instead. Three interior design motifs are offered—Contemporary, BMW M, and BMW Individual, with a choice of M Perform Tex material or Merino leather.


Prices for the new 3 Series start at $49,900 for the 330, rising to $51,900 if you want the xDrive version. Going electric will set you back $61,500 for the i3 50 xDrive, and the flagship (until the next M3 at least) M350 xDrive is $65,900. Add $1350 destination and handling before you Venmo the money to your dealer.
